Optimization sounds simple: choose the input that makes an objective as large or as small as possible. The difficulty is that real choices are rarely unlimited. A consumer maximizes utility under a budget, a firm minimizes cost while meeting a production target, and a statistician estimates parameters that must satisfy model restrictions. Lagrange multipliers provide one method for handling such constraints. The formula is familiar, but its logic can feel mysterious: why should introducing an extra variable, usually called $\lambda$, solve the problem?

## A Constraint Changes the Directions We Can Move

Consider maximizing a differentiable function $f(x,y)$ subject to

$$
g(x,y)=0.
$$

Without the constraint, an interior optimum usually satisfies $\nabla f=0$. Under a constraint, however, we are not free to move in every direction. We may move only along the curve $g(x,y)=0$.

The gradient $\nabla g$ is perpendicular to this constraint curve. Meanwhile, $\nabla f$ points in the direction in which $f$ increases most rapidly and is perpendicular to a level curve $f(x,y)=c$. If the level curve of $f$ crossed the constraint at an optimum, we could move along the constraint toward a higher level curve. Therefore, at a regular interior optimum, the two curves must be tangent. Their perpendicular vectors must consequently be parallel:

$$
\nabla f(x^*,y^*)=\lambda\nabla g(x^*,y^*).
$$

The multiplier $\lambda$ is needed because parallel vectors can have different lengths. It is the scaling factor between the two gradients.

## A Concrete Example

Suppose we want to maximize

$$
f(x,y)=xy
$$

subject to

$$
x+y=10.
$$

The level curves $xy=c$ are hyperbolas, while the constraint is a straight line. The figure shows that $xy=25$ is the highest level curve that the constraint can reach. The higher curve $xy=36$ is unattainable.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tangency
#| fig-cap: "The constraint is tangent to the highest attainable level curve at (5, 5)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

x <- seq(0.5, 10, length.out = 500)
plot(
  NA,
  xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10),
  xlab = "x", ylab = "y",
  main = "Constraint and Level Curves",
  xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i"
)
polygon(c(0, 10, 0), c(0, 0, 10), col = "#E8F1FA", border = NA)
abline(a = 10, b = -1, col = "#2166AC", lwd = 3)
lines(x, 9 / x,  col = "#67A9CF", lwd = 2)
lines(x, 25 / x, col = "#D6604D", lwd = 3)
lines(x, 36 / x, col = "#777777", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
points(5, 5, pch = 19, cex = 1.3)
text(5, 5, "  optimum (5, 5)", pos = 4)
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("x + y = 10", "xy = 9", "xy = 25", "xy = 36"),
  col = c("#2166AC", "#67A9CF", "#D6604D", "#777777"),
  lwd = c(3, 2, 3, 2), lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2),
  bty = "n"
)
```

Write the constraint as $10-x-y=0$ and form the Lagrangian

$$
\mathcal{L}(x,y,\lambda)=xy+\lambda(10-x-y).
$$

The first-order conditions are

$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=y-\lambda=0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial y}=x-\lambda=0,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\lambda}=10-x-y=0.
$$

The first two equations imply $x=y$. Combining this with $x+y=10$ gives

$$
x^*=y^*=5.
$$

Notice what differentiation with respect to $\lambda$ accomplishes: it simply restores the original constraint. We are not literally maximizing the Lagrangian over $\lambda$; instead, the Lagrangian packages the tangency condition and the constraint into one system of equations.

## The Multiplier as a Shadow Value

In this example, if the right-hand side of the constraint is a general number $I$, the optimal solution is $x=y=I/2$. The optimized objective is therefore

$$
V(I)=\frac{I^2}{4}.
$$

Its derivative at $I=10$ is

$$
V'(10)=5=\lambda.
$$

Thus $\lambda$ has a second interpretation: it measures approximately how much the best attainable objective would increase if the constraint were relaxed by one unit. This is why economists call it a *shadow value* or *shadow price*.

The method does require care. The gradients of the constraints must be well behaved, the first-order conditions identify only candidates, and boundary solutions may require additional analysis. Nevertheless, the central idea is simple and powerful: at a smooth constrained optimum, there is no feasible direction of improvement, so the objective gradient must lie in the normal direction generated by the constraint.
